content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a Controllable Adaptive Learning (CAL) paradigm that allows the model to perform well on some data domains while performing poorly on others by control. The proposed controllable module controls the model’s performance on the data. Over some data, it allows the model to show the high performance and on the other data shows lower results. The control process is unsupervised i.e. it does not require to access the label of the target data.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: 

1: The problem may have a wide application but the exact application is not clear.

2: The controlling process is interesting and also the module does not require the target data label.

3: The ablation is extensive and convincing. 

Weakness: 

1: The motivation is not clear, where and how it will be applicable to the real domain are not discussed. 

Directly I am not finding the proper use-case for the problem.

2: Writing is very poor, it looks like just written in a hurry and many sentences are incorrect or hard to understand and citations are missing. This work requires a serious editing with proper motivation. The current version is not ready to publish.

3: The problem formulation is novel, but the proposed approach is not novel. It adds the components DDE that are based on MMD. Both are very similar and do not have a significant contribution to the DDE. The prompt based controller and embedding enabled controller are somewhat novel, but without proper baseline, it is difficult to evaluate these modules. The baseline should include a few domain adaption models where they do not use the target data label. Included baseline train the model in a supervised manner and then evaluates its results on other domains that do not participate in the training. This is not a fair baseline. 

4: For the small dataset like MNIST, MNIST-M and SVHN paper use ResNet50 model, while a simple model would be sufficient. Why ResNet50 is important here?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is not clear.

Reproducibility is limited, the proper hyperparameters are not mentioned and code is not shared.

The proposed controllable module seems novel but their contribution are not clear.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper requires proper motivation with an example. Writing is very poor and many important informations are missing. It requires a serious editing. Also, the author add few recent baselines that use the unsupervised domain adaption, without strong and fair baseline its difficult to evaluate the proposed component.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies the development of controllable networks that can be trained to have poor performance on undesirable target tasks. The paper also discusses two controllers to regain performance in desired target domains. An MMD loss is introduced between the source and target features. Each sample is reweighed with a focal loss that provides a larger weight on source and target features that are "closer together." They then introduce two controllers (one based on transferring target embeddings and the other leveraging prompting). The authors show that the model is able to degrade and then recover performance on different transfer settings on MNIST and Multi-PIE.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper discusses an interesting and increasing relevant problem of safeguarding neural networks from being used for undesirable target tasks. The papers biggest weakness is a lack of comparison to baselines and a more thorough discussion from prior work. For example, [1] discusses self-destructing models that are motivated similarly as the "degraded" setting here and [2] discusses prompt tuning, which is related to the "enhanced" setting here. To recommend acceptance, I would want to see comparisons against baselines and a more in-depth discussion on related work.

[1] Self-Destructing Models: Increasing the Costs of Harmful Dual Uses in Foundation Models. https://openreview.net/pdf?id=fYPC0TnrItR
[2] The Power of Scale for Parameter-Efficient Prompt Tuning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.08691
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper would benefit from a more straightforward description of the motivation. Specifically, if the authors can develop multiple different controller types to recover performance in the target domain, doesn't that imply that the MMD degradation loss was ineffective in that an adversary would be able to develop a lightweight solution to retraining the network for a potentially harmful downstream task? I think this is an important question that the authors should address if the paper is accepted.

Minor clarity comments:
- In equation (1) the expectations are taken over only one of the random variables f or f', In the final term for the loss, there are still random variables not wrapped in an expectation. Is there an outer expectation missing?
content.summary_of_the_review: I recommend rejection because of the lack of baseline comparisons and lack of detailed discussion connecting the contributions to related work.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper introduces a novel task called Controllable Adaptive Learning (CAL) that allows the model to perform well on some data domains while performing poorly on others by control. This purpose is designed for preventing users from deploying the models from unintended uses. To achieve this goal, they design a loss called Distribution Difference Expanding (DDE) loss that exploits the idea of hard negative mining to Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD). To recover from the "Degraded" status of the target domain induced by the DDE loss, they propose two types of controllers whose existence can lift the target domain back to an "enhanced mode". The effectiveness of all proposed methods are established in their experiments.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The proposed task of preventing strong artificial intelligence systems from generalized to unintended use is novel and well-motivated. The proposed methods are also well-motivated. The paper not only considers how to set some specific target domain to "degraded" status but also considers how to set those target domain back to the "enhanced status" (with little computation) using two different methods: Embedding-enabled Controller and Prompt-based Controller.

Experiments are done on Digits and Multi-PIE datasets to show the effectiveness of the proposed methods, of both setting the target domain to "degraded" status and setting it back with two proposed controllers.

Weakness:
The writing of the "Method" section and some of the "Experiment" can be improved.

Some of the important baselines are missing in the "Experiment" section:
1) First of all, a natural concern of the CAL setting is that training with those additional losses might hurt the performance of the model on the source domain (C13 -> C13, for example). It might be a significant tradeoff for industry to consider incorporating such training in their artificial intelligence system if it hurts the performance of the model on the source domain. Therefore, results on the source domain are necessary.

2) Would like to see more baseline comparison results instead of only plain training. For example, to justify the use of MMD, maybe consider adding a baseline of using the loss of KL divergence. Maybe also consider ablating on some confidence-based methods like directly minimizing the confidence of the model on the target domain.

3) The results of "enhanced" status seems to be always better than the baseline due to domain adaptation? A justification might be needed, and also would be nice to see how the results of the "enhanced" statue compare to state-of-the-art domain adaptation methods.

4) The results of "PC" seem to always be inferior to "EC"? A justification and results may be needed to be why we need PC at all? I'm not sure what is the advantage of "PC"?

Minor:
5) This is a minor concern. Because of the light computation of "PC" and "EC", one might suspect that the introduction of "PC" and "EC" might lead to a potential weakness of the system, where adversarial users can use a small amount of data to train "PC" or "EC" to aim the artificial intelligence system for unintended use. Would be nice to see a paragraph address this concern.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The writing of the paper is good overall, but it can be improved in the Method and Experiment Section.
1) The formulation of MMD in equation (1) is unclear. Some of the notations are used without being defined. Why is f and f' sampled from a and b, a and b are distributions of what? In the first $\mathcal{H}(f, f')$, where is the f' coming from? Seems it is only sampled in the second expectation?

Minor: In section 3.1, might forget to delete "[cite]".

2) There is some redundant math here without being properly defined and motivated. I'm not sure how useful equation (3) is since here the $d_{k\delta k}$ term seems to be measuring the discrepancy between the distribution of the source and target data instead of the feature (If I understand your notation correctly). I am also not sure how useful it is of introducing the redundant parameters of the BN layer (it confuses the readers). It makes Figure 2 (a) hard to understand.

3) The introduction of "PC" seems not well-motivated. Why do we need "PC" if it is inferior to "EC" everywhere?

4) In the experiment section, for main results, it is not clear how each baseline is trained. Are they trained the same while different components like EC/PC are added only at inference time? A separate "baseline" subsection might help.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper proposes a novel and well-motivated task of Controllable Adaptive Learning that controls the performance of the model on some target domains. Proper methods are proposed and their effectiveness is established in experiments. However, there is significant improvement to be done in terms of experiments and writing. More baselines and discussions need to be done to properly evaluate their proposed method.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors proposed a Controllable Adaptive Learning (CAL) scheme to control the model performance. Specifically, they propose a Distribution Difference Expanding (DDE) Loss to restrict knowledge transfer. They then introduced two controllers, an implicit embedding-enabled controller, and an explicit prompt-based controller, to perform effective knowledge transfer.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1) The technique seems to be correct, and easy to follow.

2) The experimental results verify the effectiveness of their method.

Weakness:
1) Although the authors propose a controllable adaptive learning paradigm, it is hard to imagine what scenarios this method can be used for in real-world applications.

2) The authors proposed a loss function to prevent the knowledge transfer between source domain and target domain, in order to degrade the performance of the model. However, I do not understand why I use such a loss function to conduct knowledge transfer. As we know, there are lots of effective transfer learning methods. So it is not clear why the authors can prevent transfer learning from the deployment level, not just based on the loss function.

3). It is expected to see the convergence analysis and parameter sensitiveness analysis in their method.

4) Some relevant works are missing, e.g., Undistillable: Making A Nasty Teacher That CANNOT teach students.

5) The presentation needs to be improved, e.g., "from the target to the source domain" ->"from the source to the target domain"
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The novelty of this paper is limited, and the quality needs to be improved
content.summary_of_the_review: Because of the limited applications, I incline to reject this paper.

content.title: Controllable Adaptive Learning
content.abstract: As deep learning enabled unprecedented applications in versatile vision cognition tasks, researchers surged for the solutions of higher performance and more generalized algorithms, coming with expensive training and deployment to be applied in complex scenarios across domains. However, we argue that generalization and high performance are not always the ultimate goal in real-life with various applications and regulatory requirements. In this work, for the first time to our knowledge, we propose a Controllable Adaptive Learning (CAL) paradigm that allows the model to perform well on some data domains while performing poorly on others by control. We define the problem as a Controlled Multi-target Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (CMUDA) Task. Without the need to access labels in the target domain, we make the model perform poorly on certain target domains through a novel distribution different loss function design. We then introduced two easy-to-use control methods, namely implicit representation controller and explicit text-prompt controller, to regain access to the high-performance result with little effort, without the need to retrain the entire network. Extensive experiments demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach. We believe that our CAL paradigm will lead to an emerging trend for future research. Our code is at *URL*.
